skills.name: Use the identities for the sum and the difference of two cubes

note.text:
Two identities factorise a sum or a difference of two cubes:
• a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
• a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
Write each term as a cube first: 8 = 2³, 27x³ = (3x)³.
For example x³ − 8 = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4) and 27x³ + 1 = (3x + 1)(9x² − 3x + 1).
Sign rule: the small bracket has the same sign as the expression; the middle term of the long bracket has the opposite sign; the last term is always +.
The long bracket does not factorise further. Check by expanding.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to factorise a sum or a difference of two cubes with the right signs, and check by expanding.
Builds on: Lesson {3} (difference of two squares); Form Three cubes and cube roots.
Leads to: factorising cubic polynomials with the factor theorem and solving cubic equations.

sections.heading: Two identities
sections.text:
A cube is a number times itself three times: {2}³ = {8}, ({mono(3, 'x')})³ = {mono(27, 'x³')}.
Expand (a − b)(a² + ab + b²): a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³. Four terms cancel, leaving a³ − b³.
So:
• a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
• a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
Sign rule: the small bracket has the same sign as the expression. The middle term of the long bracket has the opposite sign. The last term is always plus.

sections.heading: Using them
sections.text:
First write each term as a cube, then read off a and b.
• {poly([1, 'x³'], [-125, ''])}: a = x, b = {5}, so ({poly([1, 'x'], [-5, ''])})({quad(1, 5, 25)}).
• {poly([8, 'x³'], [27, ''])}: a = {mono(2, 'x')}, b = {3}, so ({poly([2, 'x'], [3, ''])})({quad(4, -6, 9)}).
The long bracket never factorises further with whole numbers. Take out a common factor first if there is one: {poly([2, 'x³'], [-16, ''])} = {2}({poly([1, 'x³'], [-8, ''])}).

cards.idea: Before using an identity, write each term as a cube: {8} = {2}³, {64} = {4}³, {mono(27, 'x³')} = ({mono(3, 'x')})³.
Difference of two cubes: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
Sum of two cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²). Only the small bracket keeps the + sign.

misconceptions.explain: For a sum of cubes the middle term of the long bracket is minus: a² − ab + b².
First write {mono(k ^ 3, 'x³')} as a cube: ({mono(k, 'x')})³. Then a = {mono(k, 'x')}.

solution: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) with a = {mono(k, 'x')}, b = {1}.

misconceptions.explain: That is near the square root. The cube root of {n} is {a}, because {a} × {a} × {a} = {n}.
For a difference of cubes the long bracket is all plus: a² + ab + b².
That is the factorisation of x³ + {a ^ 3}, a sum. Here there is a minus sign.
({poly([1, 'x'], [-a, ''])})³ expands to four terms with x² and x terms. It is not x³ − {a ^ 3}.

a = x, b = {a}: a² = x², ab = {mono(a, 'x')}, b² = {a * a}.

misconceptions.explain: The middle term of the long bracket has the opposite sign to the small bracket.
(a ± b)³ expands to four terms. It is not a³ ± b³.
That identity is for squares. x³ and {a ^ 3} = {a}³ are cubes.

solution: {a ^ 3} = {a}³, so the expression is {s > 0 ? 'a sum' : 'a difference'} of two cubes.
The small bracket keeps the sign; the middle of the long bracket has the opposite sign.

questions.prompt: Given that a + b = {s} and ab = {p}, use a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) to find a³ + b³. (Hint: a² + b² = (a + b)² − {2}ab.)

misconceptions.explain: (a + b)³ is not a³ + b³: it also has the terms {3}a²b + {3}ab².
That is (a + b)(a² + b²). The long bracket is a² − ab + b²: subtract ab = {p} once more.
a² + b² is (a + b)² − {2}ab, not (a + b)²; then subtract ab.
